opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and it's one I've thought about a lot, partly because I spent so many years on the other side of the table, as a funder and as someone writing about AI risk from the outside.

The way I think about it is roughly this: I don't think the most likely path to a good outcome is that powerful AI just never gets built, or that everyone pauses indefinitely. I wish there were a clean option like that, but I don't think it's on the table. So the real question is what the world looks like as this technology gets developed, and who has influence over how it goes. A big part of that is what the leading developers actually do: what safety practices they adopt, what commitments they make, how seriously they take risks before those risks are obviously staring everyone in the face.

What I've come to believe is that there's a lot of value in a company at the frontier trying to demonstrate that you can be competitive and also take these risks seriously. It shows that safety measures are feasible, it creates templates other companies can adopt, and it gives you some credibility when you talk to policymakers about what's reasonable to ask of the industry. A lot of my work has centered on things like the idea of "if-then" commitments: if a model shows a certain dangerous capability, then you need protective measures in place before you go further. That's much easier to make real when you're inside, working on how it actually gets implemented, rather than writing essays saying someone should do it.

I want to be honest that there are real tensions here. Working at a frontier AI company means being part of the race dynamic I've worried about. There are commercial pressures, and there's a real risk that people like me tell ourselves a comfortable story about why our participation is net positive. I take that seriously. I don't think the case is a slam dunk, and I think reasonable people who care a lot about this come down differently.

But when I weigh it, I think the world where safety-focused people are absent from the frontier is worse, not better. My hope is that I can be useful by pushing on the practical details: what does a good safety framework look like, how do you make it robust to pressure, how do you get the rest of the industry and governments to raise the floor. And part of my job, as I see it, is to stay honest about whether that's working, and to say so if I come to think it isn't.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I thought about a lot, and I want to be upfront that it's not an obvious call, and I don't think reasonable people have to land where I did.

The basic case against is pretty simple: Anthropic is building the thing that I, and a lot of people in this space, think could be really dangerous. You can tell a story where every frontier lab, no matter how safety-focused, is contributing to a race dynamic, pulling capabilities forward, and making the overall situation worse. I take that story seriously. I don't think it's crazy.

But here's roughly how I ended up thinking about it. My view is that we are very likely going to get powerful AI systems whether or not any particular safety-minded person participates. The question isn't really "does this technology get built," it's "who's at the frontier when it gets built, and what are the norms, the institutions, the safety practices, and the policy environment that surround it." And on that framing, I think it matters a lot to have at least one lab at or near the frontier that's genuinely trying to take the risks seriously, that's willing to do the research on things like alignment and interpretability and evaluations, and that can be a credible voice when it talks to governments and to the rest of the industry.

I spent a long time at Open Philanthropy funding work from the outside, and I think that kind of work is really valuable. But at some point I felt like a lot of the most important questions, the ones about what actually happens inside a lab when a model shows worrying behavior, how you build a responsible scaling policy that has teeth, how you decide when to pause, were things I couldn't influence much from a grantmaker's chair. Being inside gives you a different kind of leverage. It also gives you a different kind of information. You learn what's actually hard about doing safety work when there's commercial pressure and deadlines, and that's useful even for people on the outside.

I'd also say I went in with pretty explicit conditions in my own head about what would make me think this was a mistake. If I saw the organization systematically cutting corners on safety commitments, or using "we're the responsible ones" purely as marketing cover, I'd want to leave and say so publicly. I think it's important to hold yourself to that rather than just rationalizing after the fact.

And I want to be honest about the conflict of interest. I now have a stake in Anthropic doing well, and people should discount what I say about Anthropic accordingly. I'd rather name that than pretend it isn't there.

So the short version: I don't think working at a lab is the right move for everyone concerned about AI risk, and I think the field needs plenty of people outside labs doing policy work, independent research, and holding the labs accountable. But given my particular background and the kind of influence I think I can have, I decided this was where I could do the most good. I could be wrong about that, and I try to keep checking.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a bet on where I can be useful, rather than a judgment that there’s one right place for everyone working on AI safety to be.

One reason to work at an AI company is that you’re close to the actual systems and the decisions being made about them. You can get a better sense of what’s happening, what the difficulties are, and which safety ideas can actually affect how models are developed and deployed. There’s potentially a pretty short path from doing useful work to changing an important decision.

But there are real tradeoffs. Being inside a company can shape your perspective, and the company’s interests aren’t necessarily identical to the public interest. I think you need people working independently, evaluating what companies are doing and pushing for things that companies wouldn’t choose on their own.

So for me, the question is something like: Can I contribute to concrete safety work here, do I have enough room to exercise my judgment, and does that seem more valuable than what I’d otherwise be doing? That’s a judgment I’d want to keep revisiting, rather than treating the decision to join as a permanent endorsement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a bet about where I can be useful, rather than a conclusion that working at an AI company is necessarily the best way to contribute to safety.

There’s a case for being close to where the systems are being built. You can get a better understanding of what they can do, what the next decisions are going to be, and what kinds of safety measures are actually feasible. And you have an opportunity to help turn fairly abstract concerns into concrete decisions about testing and deployment.

But there’s a real tension there, because the same organization is also advancing the technology. So I don’t think you can just say, ‘I’m working on safety, therefore my impact is positive.’ You have to ask what your work actually changes. Are you helping identify risks that otherwise would have been missed? Are you helping create conditions under which a company would slow down or decide not to deploy something?

That’s the kind of contribution I’m aiming for. And I think it’s important to keep reassessing that, rather than treating the decision to join as settling the question.
